editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.32, Definition 10.32.1 and its example distinguishing elementwise nilpotence from uniform nilpotence of ideal powers. The source explicitly defines both notions.

definitions.text: An ideal I in a commutative ring R is locally nilpotent (in the Stacks Project terminology) when each element x of I is nilpotent, with the exponent allowed to depend on x.
An ideal I of a ring R is nilpotent when there is a single positive integer n for which the product ideal I^n is the zero ideal.

editorial_reason: Read the entire Stacks 10.94 section on ascending module properties. It establishes base-change stability of flat, Mittag-Leffler, direct-sum-of-countably-generated, and projective modules in Lemma 10.94.1; it does not introduce a standalone formal definition of an 'ascending property' in that section. This topic is therefore retained as a theorem/research lead, not a fabricated new definition.

Read Stacks 10.35, Definition 10.35.1 and Lemmas 10.35.3–10.35.4. They distinguish the radical-ideal definition and the equivalent characterization using prime ideals, with the geometric formulation via closed points of the spectrum.

definitions.text: A commutative ring R is a Jacobson ring when every radical ideal I of R equals the intersection of the maximal ideals of R containing I.
Equivalently, a commutative ring R is Jacobson if each prime ideal p is the intersection of all maximal ideals containing p.

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 9.22, especially Lemma 9.22.1 defining the canonical profinite topology through continuity of the Galois action on the discretely topologized field. This supplies a precise concept under the chapter topic, rather than treating 'infinite Galois theory' as a new object.

definitions.text: For a Galois extension E/F, the Krull topology on Gal(E/F) is the weakest topology making every evaluation map sigma ↦ sigma(a), for a in E, continuous when E is discrete. With this topology the Galois group is profinite.
definitions.context_hint: Infinite Galois theory: Krull topology on an absolute or relative Galois group

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 5.16, Lemma 5.16.1, which characterizes constructible subsets in Noetherian topological spaces exactly as finite unions of locally closed subsets. Its context is explicitly Noetherian.

definitions.text: If X is a Noetherian topological space, a subset C of X is constructible exactly when C can be expressed as a finite union of sets U∩F, where U is open in X and F is closed in X.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: constructible subset of a Noetherian space

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.120, Definitions 10.120.1, 10.120.4, 10.120.12, and 10.120.14. The section introduces distinct basic notions of element factorization and ring types; they are recorded as different contexts, not a single interchangeable meaning.

definitions.text: Two elements a and b of an integral domain R are associates if a=ub for some invertible element u of R.
definitions.context_hint: Factorization in integral domains: associate elements

definitions.text: An element r of an integral domain R is irreducible if it is nonzero and not a unit and every factorization r=ab has at least one unit factor.
definitions.context_hint: Factorization in integral domains: irreducible element

definitions.text: A nonzero nonunit element p of an integral domain R is a prime element when the principal ideal (p) is a prime ideal; equivalently, p divides ab only if p divides a or p divides b.
definitions.context_hint: Factorization in integral domains: prime element

definitions.text: An integral domain R is a unique factorization domain when every nonzero nonunit factors into finitely many irreducibles, and any two such factorizations agree after reordering factors and multiplying them by units.
An integral domain R is a principal ideal domain if every ideal of R can be generated by a single element.

An integral domain R is a Dedekind domain in this factorization characterization if every nonzero ideal factors as a finite product of nonzero prime ideals and this decomposition is unique up to permuting the factors.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: ideal-factorization characterization of Dedekind domain

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.73 in full. Its 'Functorialities for Ext' section lists constructions and proves a flat-base-change isomorphism for Ext groups, but does not introduce a new standalone mathematical definition for the chapter heading. The Ext functor itself belongs to a separately cited construction.

Read Stacks 10.116 on dimension of finite-type algebras over fields. The chapter establishes equalities between Krull dimension and transcendence degree, including Lemma 10.116.1, but does not define a new concept named 'dimension ... reprise'. The constituent established definitions need their original defining sections.

Read Stacks 10.21 and Lemmas 10.21.1, 10.21.3, and 10.21.4. The page proves that clopen subsets of Spec(R) correspond uniquely to ring idempotents, providing a precise equivalent specification of these subsets.

definitions.text: For a commutative ring R, a subset U of Spec(R) is simultaneously open and closed exactly when there is an idempotent e of R (so e²=e) such that U=D(e)={p in Spec(R):e is not in p}; this e is unique.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: clopen subsets of an affine spectrum

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 4.26, Definition 4.26.1, stating that a categorically compact object is one for which its represented Hom functor commutes with existing filtered colimits.

definitions.text: In a category C, an object X is categorically compact if for every filtered diagram M_i whose colimit exists, the natural map colim_i Hom_C(X,M_i) → Hom_C(X,colim_i M_i) is bijective.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: categorically compact or finitely presentable object

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 4.30, Definition 4.30.1, whose sole explicit new categorical concept is a strict (2,1)-category. The invertibility requirement applies to 2-morphisms, not to arbitrary 1-morphisms.

definitions.text: A strict (2,1)-category is a strict 2-category in which each 2-morphism is invertible with respect to vertical composition, so every hom-category is a groupoid.

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.151, Definition 10.151.1 and Lemma 10.151.2. This section explicitly contrasts unramified and G-unramified maps, including local conditions at a prime of the target ring, all using Kähler differentials.

definitions.text: A homomorphism of commutative rings R→S is unramified in the Stacks Project convention when S is finitely generated as an R-algebra and the module of Kähler differentials Ω_{S/R} is zero.
A ring homomorphism R→S is G-unramified in the Stacks Project convention if it is of finite presentation and Ω_{S/R}=0.
For a ring map R→S and a prime ideal q in S, the map is unramified at q if some g in S outside q makes the localized map R→S_g unramified.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: unramified at a target prime

definitions.text: For a ring map R→S and prime q of S, the map is G-unramified at q if there exists g outside q such that R→S_g is G-unramified.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: G-unramified at a target prime
